long_biography.plain_text:
On 28 April 1919, Leslie Leroy Irvin stepped from an Army aircraft over McCook Field without a static line. Using a manually operated parachute designed by Floyd Smith and Guy Ball, he completed the first successful intentional Army freefall test. The landing broke his ankle, but the demonstration disproved fears that a falling person could not remain conscious and deploy a chute.

Irvin had learned aerial risk as a teenage balloon parachutist and Hollywood stunt performer. Within months of the test, he founded Irving Air Chute Company in Buffalo and became its president and chief engineer. The business expanded internationally, reaching six factories by the eve of the Second World War. Irvin's organisation also established the Caterpillar Club for people whose lives were saved by emergency parachute descents. As wartime supply conditions changed, his company helped move parachute canopies from silk to nylon, extending a career built around making escape from aircraft more reliable.
